children: The rupee has gained more than 1% this week, breaking below the 95-per-dollar mark and rising to a two-month high, helped by a much larger-than-expected $136.4 billion of inflows through the RBI’s special concessional window over the past two months. But analysts believe the currency’s gains could be difficult to sustain, with the support from these inflows set to fade after the swap settlement process and rising crude prices adding fresh pressure.
$136 billion inflows give rupee a boost

The rupee saw its strongest close on Thursday in about 10 weeks, after gaining 49 paise in a single session. The currency has now gained more than 1% this week, making it Asia’s second-best performing currency after the Korean won.

The key support has come from the large foreign currency inflows mobilised through the RBI’s special concessional window. The total inflow has reached $136.4 billion, significantly higher than market expectations. A softer dollar has also helped the rupee’s recent gains.
However, analysts say the strength may not last once the flow-related support starts to fade.
September 11 could be a key test

Amit Pabari, managing director at CR Forex, said FCNR(B)-related conversions and active RBI support are currently helping anchor the rupee, but higher crude prices and elevated US yields remain key risks.
He expects underlying demand for dollars from importers to return as the swap settlement process approaches completion after September 11.
Pabari sees immediate support for the rupee at 94.35-94.50, but expects the dollar-rupee pair to move back towards 95.50-96.00 as the impact of the swap-related flows gradually fades.
Oil is another headache
The rupee’s recent strength has come despite a sharp rise in crude prices.

Brent crude moved past $96 a barrel on Friday and is headed for its biggest weekly gain since mid-July as renewed US-Iran hostilities raised concerns over oil supplies from the Middle East. Brent was up more than 7% for the week.
Higher oil prices are a negative for the rupee because India imports a large share of its crude requirement, increasing the country’s demand for dollars.
The rise in oil prices has also pushed up concerns around inflation and US interest rates, adding another layer of uncertainty for emerging-market currencies.
US rate outlook remains another risk

Markets are also closely watching the US Federal Reserve’s next policy decision. Fed Governor Christopher Waller said on Thursday that he could support keeping rates unchanged if upcoming inflation data continues to show improvement, but would consider a rate hike if inflation comes in stronger than expected. The Fed’s next meeting is scheduled for September 15-16.

Waller’s comments have eased some of the rate-hike bets that had built up after Fed Chair Kevin Warsh’s more hawkish remarks at Jackson Hole. That has provided some relief to the dollar and, in turn, supported the rupee.
However, a stronger-than-expected US inflation or jobs reading could revive expectations of higher US rates and put pressure on the rupee.
Analysts see limited upside from here

Dilip Parmar, senior research analyst at HDFC Securities, said the dollar-rupee pair’s technical setup has weakened, with a pattern of lower highs and lower lows. He sees immediate support at 94.10 and resistance at 94.95.

Jateen Trivedi, vice president and research analyst at LKP Securities, expects the rupee to retain a positive bias in the near term, with the currency likely to trade in the 94.25-95.00 range. He said traders will closely track US jobs data, particularly non-farm payrolls and unemployment figures, for clues on the Fed’s next move.
The rupee’s move below 95 is a significant near-term improvement, but analysts see the rally as increasingly dependent on factors that may not last.

title: Rupee hits 2-month high; analysts warn pressure may return after swap ends, oil prices surge
